newsitem.title: UK: Euro contracts have few snags in Japan -law panel.
newsitem.headline: Euro contracts have few snags in Japan -law panel.

text.p: Japanese courts are likely to pursue continuity of contracts after a European single currency is launched, a London-based industry panel said on Wednesday.
But the Financial Law Panel (FLP), sponsored by the Corporation of London and the Bank of England, found there could be some exceptions where the contract would cease to be binding.

"The doctrines which might dilute the effect of continuity of contract are likely to apply only in very limited circumstances," said the Panel in the first of a series of five studies examining the continuity of contracts outside the European Union.
The analysis on Japan was prepared with the help of officials from the Japanese Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Japan and two of Tokyo's leading commercial law firms.

The FLP said commercial public opinion in Japan would be disturbled by a court decision which produced a result which was different from that which applied in the countries whose currencies were concerned.

Japanese lawyers reckoned that that the principle of "lex monetae" applies, so that legal issues relating to a foreign currency are to be determined by the law of the country whose currency is involved. It was generally accepted that payment obligations could never become impossible to perform, either legally or physically.
But where the foreign currency is involved as a reference point, or is itself the object of the contract, continuity could bump into the so-called "doctrine of change of circumstances".
For example, in the case of a currency swap, change of circumstances could apply on the grounds that purpose of the contract was frustrated.

"It is thought unlikely, however, that a Japanese court would be attracted to this view," said the panel, adding that the economic consequence would need to be very great before the doctrine would be invoked.

But it noted Japanese courts might hesitate to grant continuity of contracts if it was felt that the rules of EU countries which applied to contracts governed by Japanese law had been set unreasonably.
